The core of scientific data analysis lies in measuring, quantifying, and reasoning about uncertainty. Throughout this textbook, we develop machine learning methods based on Bayesian principles. These methods help us understand astronomical phenomena under uncertainty. Before we apply them, we must establish the probability theory behind the Bayesian approach.

Inference means drawing conclusions about unknown quantities, such as model parameters, from measured data. Bayesian inference treats both observations and model parameters as random variables. Treating observations as random seems intuitive, because our measurements have uncertainty. Treating model parameters as random may seem odd. Physical constants like the gravitational constant, or the mass of a galaxy, should have definite values. Yet our knowledge of these values is uncertain, and Bayesian inference gives a consistent way to update that knowledge as we collect more observations.

This view is especially useful in astronomy, where we cannot repeat many phenomena under controlled conditions. Astronomers often study unique events and have limited data. Treating model parameters as random variables lets us make statements about uncertainty even when we have limited data.

In this chapter, we start with deterministic and random variables, then cover the probability distributions common in astronomy and the rules for manipulating probabilities. We then compare frequentist and Bayesian approaches and show how Bayesian inference works in practice, even with minimal data. Many methods, from linear regression to neural networks, extend one Bayesian idea. This idea is to update our beliefs about model parameters using observed data.

2.1 Deterministic vs. Random Variables

To see why scientific inference needs a probabilistic approach, we first distinguish between deterministic and random variables.

Deterministic Variables are quantities that yield the same value under the same conditions. For example, the orbital period of a planet around a star of known mass at a known distance follows deterministic physical laws. By “the same conditions” we mean that we specify and fix all relevant physical parameters. Kepler’s Third Law for a planet orbiting a star is \[ P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3. \] Here \(P\) is the orbital period, \(G\) is the gravitational constant, and \(a\) is the semi-major axis of the orbit. \(M\) is the mass of the central star, which we assume is much larger than the mass of the planet (\(M \gg m_\text{planet}\)).

The variables \(P\), \(M\), and \(a\) are deterministic variables. If we specify \(M\) and \(a\), they completely determine the period \(P\). If we use the same values for \(M\) and \(a\) again, we obtain exactly the same period \(P\). Most quantities in basic physics and mathematics courses are deterministic in this way. Consider solving the equation \[ x^2 + 2x - 3 = 0. \]

The solutions \(x = 1\) and \(x = -3\) are deterministic. They are the exact values that satisfy the equation, and they do not change however many times we solve it.

Random Variables, in contrast, are quantities whose values are subject to uncertainty or variation. Even when we specify all known conditions, we can only predict probabilities of different outcomes, not the exact outcome. In astronomy, the true orbital period of a planet is deterministic, but our measurement of it is a random variable. To measure the period \(P\), we make many observations of the star’s radial velocity or the planet’s transit. Each measurement has some uncertainty from instrumental noise and atmospheric effects. Our final estimate of \(P\) comes with an uncertainty, often written as \(P \pm \sigma_P\).

This uncertainty does not arise because the true period is random. The randomness comes from our imperfect measurement process.

Random variables come in two main forms.

Random by Nature

Some quantities appear to be probabilistic at the most basic level, such as quantum phenomena. Examples include the exact time of decay of a radioactive atom and the spin measurement of an electron in a superposition state.

Incomplete Knowledge or Measurement Uncertainty

Many astronomical quantities appear random because of practical limits, not because they are probabilistic. Consider again the orbital period, which Kepler’s Third Law fixes exactly for given values of mass and semi-major axis. Our measurements of these quantities still have uncertainties. The star’s mass may have error bars from spectroscopic analysis, and observational limits may affect the semi-major axis.

The true period is a fixed value, but because our inputs and our period measurements are uncertain, we can only make probabilistic statements about it. This turning of deterministic quantities into random variables is common in astronomical analysis. Figure 2.1 contrasts a true value with the distribution of its measurements.

This distinction matters when we analyze physical systems. We often know the physical laws, such as Kepler’s Third Law, but our measurements of the parameters are uncertain. This creates an asymmetry in scientific inference. We can easily predict the observations that a given set of parameters should produce, which is the forward problem. Finding the parameters from the observations, which is the inverse problem, requires us to include the sources of uncertainty.

For instance, the mass of the black hole at the center of a galaxy has a definite value. Our estimate of this mass, based on stellar velocities, gas dynamics, or other techniques, has uncertainty. We represent this uncertainty with a probability distribution that describes our current knowledge. As we gather more data, this distribution becomes narrower around the true value, but some uncertainty remains.

Describing our knowledge of physical quantities with probability distributions gives a consistent mathematical language for scientific inference. We start with prior knowledge, add new observations, and update our understanding step by step.

2.2 Probability Distributions

We now need a mathematical way to describe the uncertainty of these random variables. Probability distributions do this. They describe how probability is spread over the possible values of a random variable.

A probability distribution describes our state of knowledge about a parameter such as the mass of a black hole. It does not mean that the mass itself fluctuates. Its peak marks our best estimate, and its width shows our uncertainty. For observational data, it describes both the expected value and the uncertainty of our measurements.

An event \(A\) is a set of possible values of a random variable \(X\), such as a measured period between 365.2 and 365.3 days. We write its probability as \(P(A)\). This probability must satisfy three axioms.

  1. Non-negativity means \(P(A) \geq 0\) for any event \(A\)

  2. Normalization means \(P(\Omega) = 1\), where \(\Omega\) is the sample space, which contains all possible outcomes

  3. Additivity means that for mutually exclusive events \(A\) and \(B\), which cannot both happen, \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\), where \(A \cup B\) means that \(A\) or \(B\) happens

A probability gives one number for a specific event. A probability distribution covers all possible values of a random variable at once. This concept is central to statistical inference because it gives a complete description of uncertainty rather than a single-point estimate.

Astronomy has both discrete and continuous random variables, which we treat differently.

Discrete Case

Some astronomical quantities take only specific, countable values. Examples are photon counts in a given time interval and galaxy morphological types, such as spiral, elliptical, or irregular. For a discrete random variable \(X\), we define a probability mass function (PMF) \(p(x)\) where

  • \(p(x) = P(X = x)\) is the probability of \(X\) taking the specific value \(x\)

  • \(\sum_x p(x) = 1\) (normalization)

Continuous Case

Most astronomical measurements are continuous. For these random variables, we define a probability density function (PDF) \(p(x)\) where

  • \(P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b p(x)\mathrm{d}x\) is the probability of \(X\) falling in the interval \([a,b]\)

  • \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x)\mathrm{d}x = 1\) (normalization)

A random variable \(X\) does not take a fixed value. It follows a probability distribution, and we write this as \[ X \sim P(x). \] This notation says concisely that the random variable follows that distribution.

A subtle point about continuous distributions is that the probability of measuring any exact value is zero. If we measured an orbital period with infinite precision, what would be the probability of getting exactly 365.256363... days? There are infinitely many possible values, so the probability of any specific one is zero. We can only discuss the probability that a measurement falls in an interval, such as between 365.2 and 365.3 days. We find it by integrating the PDF. The value of \(p(x)\) itself gives the relative density of measurements near \(x\).

This has an implication for inference with continuous parameters. When a probability distribution peaks at a certain value, it marks the most likely small range of values around that point. The shape of the distribution around the peak shows the uncertainty. A narrow peak means high confidence, and a broad distribution means greater uncertainty.

2.3 Common Distributions in Astronomy

Several probability distributions appear often in astronomy. We can derive some of them, such as the Gaussian, from the principle of maximum entropy. Entropy measures how uncertain a distribution is (Section 8.6). The principle picks the most uncertain distribution that still matches the constraints we know, such as a given mean and variance. We can also understand where these distributions come from through physical intuition, which shows when and why they arise.

Gaussian Distribution

The Gaussian or normal distribution arises when we only know, or constrain, the mean and variance of a quantity. Physically, it appears when many small, independent effects add together (Section 2.5.1 defines independence). The Central Limit Theorem explains this. Consider measuring a star’s brightness, where the measurement has countless sources of uncertainty.

For a single random variable \(X\), we write \[ X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2) \] to denote that it follows a Gaussian distribution with probability density \[ p(x|\mu,\sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]Here, \(p(x|\mu,\sigma)\) is the probability density at value \(x\) given parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), where

  • \(x\) is the random variable (e.g., the measured brightness)

  • \(\mu\) is the mean or expected value

  • \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation (Chapter 3), measuring the spread of the distribution

  • The factor \(1/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\) normalizes the total probability to 1

To see why Gaussian distributions are so common in astronomical measurements, consider how we measure stellar brightness. Many small air pockets of varying density and temperature disturb each photon’s path through the atmosphere. The telescope’s optics add small aberrations from surface imperfections and thermal variations. The detector adds electronic noise from millions of independent electron movements in the CCD, and the analog-to-digital conversion adds quantization noise.

Each effect is small and independent, but they add up. By the Central Limit Theorem, a sum of many small, independent effects approaches a Gaussian distribution, whatever their individual distributions. Figure 2.2 shows the standard Gaussian.

This is why the Gaussian distribution is so common in nature. It is the choice that adds the fewest assumptions when we know only the mean and variance. It is also the result when many small, independent effects combine and nothing else constrains them.

For multivariate data, meaning many different random variables, we write \[ \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \] to denote a multivariate Gaussian distribution with probability density \[ p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right). \]In this expression

  • \(\mathbf{x}\) is a \(D\)-dimensional vector of random variables

  • \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is the mean vector

  • \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the \(D \times D\) covariance matrix

  • \(\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is the determinant of the covariance matrix

  • \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) is the inverse of the covariance matrix

The covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) holds the variance of each variable (diagonal elements) and also how pairs of variables are correlated (off-diagonal elements). This matters for multivariate astronomical data, such as the correlation between different spectral lines or between mass, age, and metallicity in stellar populations.

Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution arises when we count independent events that occur at a constant average rate and we know only the mean rate. It is central to photon detection and many other counting processes in astronomy. Its probability mass function for \(k\) events at the mean rate \(\lambda\) is \[ P(X=k|\lambda) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}. \]

To see how the Poisson distribution arises from physical principles, consider detecting photons from a distant star. We divide the observation time into short intervals, so that the chance of two or more photons in one interval is negligible. Three principles then apply, namely independence, uniformity, and randomness.

Photon arrivals in different intervals are independent, so one arrival has no effect on another. The chance of detecting a photon in an interval is proportional to its length, so doubling an interval’s length doubles its chance. Finally, the arrival times are random, since no two photons arrive at exactly the same instant and no times are preferred. Figure 2.3 shows the Poisson distribution.

These simple assumptions lead to the Poisson distribution, which describes random, independent counting events. This is why photon counts, cosmic ray hits, and galaxy counts in small volumes tend to follow Poisson statistics.

The Poisson distribution is closely related to the Gaussian distribution. When the mean rate \(\lambda\) is large, the Poisson distribution approaches a Gaussian with mean \(\mu=\lambda\) and variance \(\sigma^2=\lambda\). This is a special case of the Central Limit Theorem. In astronomy, photon counting follows Poisson statistics, but for bright sources with high count rates we can often approximate the counts with a Gaussian. Figure 2.4 shows how the Poisson distribution approaches the Gaussian.

Power Law Distribution

Power laws appear when a process has no characteristic scale, so the physics works the same way regardless of size. An example is the mass distribution of stars, the Initial Mass Function, for a stellar mass \(x\) and a power-law index \(\alpha\) \[ p(x) \propto x^{-\alpha}. \]

When physical limits restrict \(x\) to a range between \(x_{\min}\) and \(x_{\max}\), the normalized power law is \[ p(x) = \frac{1-\alpha}{x_{\max}^{1-\alpha} - x_{\min}^{1-\alpha}} x^{-\alpha}. \] The prefactor makes the integral of \(p(x)\) from \(x_{\min}\) to \(x_{\max}\) equal to 1.

Why do power laws arise in star formation? Consider the fragmentation of a molecular cloud. As a massive cloud collapses under its own gravity, it becomes unstable and fragments into smaller clouds. Each of these can fragment again through the same physical processes. The physics of this fragmentation stays similar at different size scales.

The same processes drive the fragmentation in a massive cloud complex of hundreds of parsecs and in a small protostellar core of 0.01 parsecs. Gravitational collapse competes with turbulent pressure, magnetic fields add support, and thermal pressure from heating and cooling affects the dynamics. The cloud does not “know” whether it is breaking into pieces of 1 parsec or 0.1 parsec. The process looks nearly the same at different scales, within the limits set by the interstellar medium. Figure 2.5 shows the Initial Mass Function.

Power laws also appear in many other astronomical settings. Galaxy luminosity functions, the distribution of cosmic structures, and the energy distributions of particles in astrophysical plasmas often follow power laws. This shows the scale-invariant nature of many astronomical processes, where similar mechanisms operate over many orders of magnitude.

2.4 Joint and Conditional Probability

Real astronomical problems involve several variables at once. Even with one parameter and one observable, we have a pair of related random variables that we must analyze together. So we need to understand how random variables relate to each other.

In practice, astronomical problems have many more dimensions. To characterize a stellar spectrum, we need several parameters for the physical properties of the star. These include its effective temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, rotational velocity, and possibly magnetic field strength. Our data are flux measurements at thousands of wavelengths, each with its own uncertainty. This creates a web of relationships between many variables that we must untangle statistically.

We therefore manipulate these variables in different ways. Sometimes we want the observations we expect for given model parameters, which is the forward problem. At other times we want to infer model parameters from observations, which is the inverse problem. To handle both, we need joint and conditional probabilities.

Joint Probability

For two random variables \(x\) and \(y\), the joint probability distribution \(p(x,y)\) gives the probability that both variables take specific values at the same time. We look at both the discrete and the continuous case in astronomy.

For discrete variables, joint probability is simple. Consider classifying galaxies by morphology (spiral or elliptical) and size (large or small). Here \(p(\text{spiral}, \text{large})\) is the probability of finding a galaxy that is both spiral and large. It measures how often this combination occurs in the galaxy population.

The concept extends to continuous variables. Consider stars described by temperature and luminosity. The joint distribution \(p(T,L)\) gives the probability density of finding stars in the temperature-luminosity space, which produces the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Not all combinations are equally likely. Stars cluster along the main sequence, which follows from the physics of stellar evolution.

As for single continuous variables, the probability of any exact pair of values is zero. To get meaningful probabilities, we integrate over finite regions. For example, the probability of finding a star with temperature between \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) and luminosity between \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) is \[ P(T_1 \leq T \leq T_2, L_1 \leq L \leq L_2) = \int_{L_1}^{L_2} \int_{T_1}^{T_2} p(T,L) \, \mathrm{d}T \, \mathrm{d}L. \]

Conditional Probability

Joint probability describes two events that occur together. Conditional probability asks a different question. Given that we know one event has occurred, what is the probability of another? We write this as \(p(x|y)\), read as “the probability of \(x\) given \(y\).”

Consider again the stars. The joint distribution \(p(T,L)\) describes the overall distribution of stars in temperature-luminosity space. Now suppose we observe a star and measure its temperature precisely. The conditional probability \(p(L|T)\) gives the distribution of possible luminosities for stars at that temperature. This “slice” through the joint distribution at fixed temperature usually covers a much narrower range of luminosities than the range for all stars. Figure 2.6 shows the joint distribution and such a slice.

Conditional probability is central to statistical inference. Two conditional probabilities describe the relationship between the forward and inverse problems.

  • In the forward problem, we know the model parameters and ask what observations to expect. This is \(p(\text{data}|\text{model})\).

  • In the inverse problem, we have the observations and ask what they tell us about the model parameters. This is \(p(\text{model}|\text{data})\).

2.5 Probability Rules and Independence

We now look at the rules that connect these probabilities. They are the basis of statistical inference and lead to one of the most important results in probability theory, Bayes’ theorem.

The Sum Rule

We often want information about a single variable from a joint distribution of several variables. Suppose we have the joint distribution \(p(T,L)\) of stellar temperature and luminosity, but we only want the distribution of luminosities, whatever the temperature. How do we get it?

The answer is the marginal distribution and the sum rule. A marginal distribution describes one variable while we include all possible values of the other variables. The sum rule tells us how to compute it. Summing or integrating over the variables we do not need is called marginalization.

For discrete variables, the probability that \(X\) takes a specific value \(x\) is the sum over all possible values of \(Y\) \[ p(x) = \sum_y p(x,y). \]

For continuous variables, as in our stellar example, we integrate over all possible values of the other variable \[ p(L) = \int p(T,L) \, \mathrm{d}T. \]Here \(p(L)\) is the probability of finding a star with luminosity \(L\), whatever its temperature. We can picture this as “collapsing” the two-dimensional joint distribution along the temperature axis. Figure 2.7 shows this for a bivariate Gaussian.

Marginalization is important for multivariate data. A study of galaxies may have a joint distribution of several properties, such as mass, star formation rate, and metallicity. The sum rule gives the distribution of any one property by integrating over the others. This helps when we want to compare our results with earlier studies that used different subsets of properties.

The Product Rule

The product rule relates joint probabilities to conditional probabilities \[ p(x,y) = p(x|y)p(y) = p(y|x)p(x). \]

To see this, consider our stellar example. We can split the joint probability \(p(T,L)\) of finding a star with temperature \(T\) and luminosity \(L\) in two equivalent ways.

1. First take the probability \(p(T)\) of a star with temperature \(T\), then multiply by the probability \(p(L|T)\) of luminosity \(L\) at that temperature \[ p(T,L) = p(L|T)p(T). \]

2. Or first take the probability \(p(L)\) of a star with luminosity \(L\), then multiply by the probability \(p(T|L)\) of temperature \(T\) at that luminosity \[ p(T,L) = p(T|L)p(L). \]

The equality of these two expressions, \(p(L|T)p(T) = p(T|L)p(L)\), matters more than it first appears. Stellar evolution gives the probability of a luminosity for a given temperature, \(p(L|T)\). But we may want to infer temperature from an observed luminosity, \(p(T|L)\). The product rule shows that these viewpoints are connected. We can convert between them if we know the overall distributions of temperature and luminosity in the stellar population.

The conditional probabilities \(p(L|T)\) and \(p(T|L)\) are generally not equal. Knowing the probability of luminosity given temperature does not directly give the probability of temperature given luminosity. For example, a star with temperature 6000K might have an 80% chance of a luminosity between 0.5 and 2 solar luminosities. But a star with 1 solar luminosity might have only a 30% chance of a temperature between 5800 and 6200K.

This asymmetry is at the heart of scientific inference. Our theories predict observables from physical parameters (forward direction), but we observe phenomena and want their physical properties (inverse direction). The product rule and the sum rule together give the mathematical basis for connecting these two perspectives.

2.5.1 Independence

Before we connect the product rule to statistical inference, we look at one more useful concept, independence, which we will meet often in this book. When we have many variables, it helps to know whether we can handle them separately without changing the conclusion of the inference.

Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if knowing the value of one gives no information about the other. In other words, observing \(Y\) does not change our probability for \(X\) \[ P(X|Y) = P(X) \quad \text{for all values of } Y. \]This definition matches our intuition. If knowing \(Y\) tells us nothing new about \(X\), the probability of \(X\) stays the same for any value of \(Y\) that we observe.

From this definition and the product rule, we can derive another property of independent variables. Recall that the product rule gives \[ P(X,Y) = P(X|Y)P(Y). \] If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(P(X|Y) = P(X)\), so \[ P(X,Y) = P(X)P(Y). \]So for independent variables, the joint probability factorizes into a product of individual probabilities. Many texts use this factorization as the definition of independence. Here it follows from the more intuitive definition through conditional probabilities. Figure 2.8 contrasts independent and dependent variables.

For continuous random variables, the same equations hold with probability densities in place of probabilities. Independence still means that knowing one variable tells us nothing about the other \[ p(x|y) = p(x) \quad \text{leads to} \quad p(x,y) = p(x)p(y). \]

Consider photons from two widely separated stars. The arrival time of a photon from one star is independent of the arrivals from the other. Detecting a photon from the first star tells us nothing about when we detect one from the second. Similarly, star counts in non-overlapping regions of the sky that are far enough apart are independent. So we can analyze different patches of the sky separately when we study stellar populations. In contrast, the temperature and luminosity of a star are not independent, because a star’s temperature tells us much about its likely luminosity.

Independence simplifies analysis. When random variables are independent, we can analyze them separately. For example, for multiple independent measurements of the same quantity, the joint probability of all measurements is the product of the individual probabilities. This helps with large datasets, because we can break a complex problem into simpler pieces.

We must not assume independence without justification, because many astronomical properties are correlated in subtle ways. In galaxy surveys, for example, neighboring galaxies often have correlated properties because they share an environment and formation history. Knowing when we can assume independence is important for sound statistical analysis in astronomy.

The sum rule, the product rule, and independence are the tools we need for inference with astronomical data. The product rule leads directly to Bayes’ theorem, which we derive below.

2.6 Frequentist and Bayesian Approaches

We can now compare two approaches to statistical inference, frequentist and Bayesian. The choice affects how we approach machine learning in astronomy, and astronomical problems often favor a Bayesian perspective.

The Frequentist Approach

The frequentist approach, as its name suggests, defines probability through repeated experiments, that is, through frequency. Consider whether a die is fair. A frequentist rolls the die many times and plots the relative frequency of each outcome. For a fair die, these frequencies converge to 1/6 for each face as the number of rolls grows. This convergence is the law of large numbers. It is the basis of frequentist probability, because with enough trials the sample average approaches the true population parameter.

This approach is intuitive as well as mathematically sound. In many areas of science, especially laboratory physics, we can repeat experiments many times under controlled conditions. Each trial is independent, and our statistical uncertainties shrink in proportion to \(1/\sqrt{N}\), where \(N\) is the number of measurements. Section 3.6 derives this scaling. The Central Limit Theorem adds that the average of many measurements follows a nearly Gaussian distribution.

The confidence interval is a good example of the frequentist approach. A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeated our experiment many times, about 95% of similarly constructed intervals would contain the true parameter value. This statement describes the long-run behavior of the procedure. It does not give our degree of belief in the parameter value itself.

In astronomy, we often cannot repeat an observation. For cosmological parameters such as the densities of dark matter and dark energy, we have only one observable universe. Many questions concern unique objects or events, such as the Milky Way’s central black hole, a particular supernova, or the Solar System’s formation. In these cases, the repeated experiment is only hypothetical, which makes the frequentist interpretation hard to apply.

Frequentist methods remain useful in astronomy, for example for large surveys with many similar objects and for random measurement errors. However, these limits explain why astronomers often need tools beyond frequentist methods, particularly for unique systems or complex systematic uncertainties. This leads us to the Bayesian approach.

The Bayesian Approach

Bayesian inference asks what we can infer about the physical system from our current knowledge and observations. It also asks how we should update this inference when new data arrive. In the frequentist approach, parameters are fixed unknown numbers and only the data are random. The central insight of Thomas Bayes was to treat the observations and the model parameters as random variables on equal footing. Both play similar roles, like two sides of the same coin.

Treating model parameters as uncertain may seem unsettling. In physics and astronomy, we believe that true physical laws describe how the universe works. Examples are the equation of state of dark energy, the mass of the Milky Way’s central black hole, and the mechanism that drives galaxy evolution. The Bayesian view does not deny that these truths exist. It says that our knowledge of them is uncertain, because our observations and theory are incomplete. With finite samples, as with our one observable universe, or with systematic uncertainties, we cannot be certain about our models.

Our “belief” in a theory is therefore itself a random variable. The probability distribution that represents our state of knowledge becomes more narrowly peaked as evidence accumulates, but some uncertainty remains. This matches how science progresses, by continued refinement of our understanding as new evidence narrows our uncertainty.

Mathematical Formalism

Bayes’ theorem follows directly from the probability rules above. For two random variables \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\), the product rule gives two equivalent ways to write their joint probability \[ p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})p(\mathbf{y}) = p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}). \]This symmetry in the product rule leads directly to Bayes’ theorem. Since both expressions equal the joint probability, we can write \[ p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})p(\mathbf{y}) = p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x}). \] Dividing both sides by \(p(\mathbf{y})\) gives \[ p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{y})}. \]

Because \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are both random variables, neither plays a privileged role, and we can reverse the direction of conditioning. This is useful because it lets us infer model parameters from data. We apply Bayes’ theorem to astronomical research by writing \(\mathcal{D}\) for the observational data and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) for the model parameters. Both can be complex. \(\mathcal{D}\) might contain millions of data points from a large survey, and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) might contain hundreds of parameters that describe detailed physical processes. Bayes’ theorem then becomes \[ p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{p(\mathcal{D})}. \]

Terms of Bayes’ Theorem

This equation may look like simple algebra, but each term has a specific meaning in scientific inference.

  1. \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{D})\) is the posterior distribution. It represents our updated knowledge about the model parameters after seeing the data. It tells us which combinations of parameters are most likely to explain our observations. The posterior distribution gives a complete picture of our uncertainty about the parameters, in addition to the best-fit values.

  2. \(p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})\) is the likelihood function. It measures how well our model explains the observed data. For a specific choice of model parameters, how likely are we to observe the data we measured? The likelihood function connects model predictions to reality. We read it as a function of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) with the data held fixed. It need not integrate to one over \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).

  3. \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is our prior distribution. It encodes what we know about the model parameters before we consider the data. This may include knowing that some parameter values are physically unreasonable, or that previous studies suggest a range. The prior lets us add existing scientific knowledge formally.

  4. \(p(\mathcal{D})\) is the evidence. It is the probability of the data after we average over the parameter values, weighted by the prior. For continuous parameters, the sum rule and the product rule give \(p(\mathcal{D}) = \int p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \, \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\). This quantity is also called the marginal likelihood. It matters for model comparison, and it acts as a normalization constant when we estimate parameters.

We return to the evidence \(p(\mathcal{D})\) when we discuss information criteria and model selection in Section 11.8. Because it does not depend on \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), it is a constant in parameter estimation. In this book and in many practical applications, we therefore often use the proportional form \[ p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) p(\boldsymbol{\theta}). \]

To see how Bayes’ theorem guides scientific inference, imagine we propose a set of model parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). We can ask how likely we are to observe our actual data \(\mathcal{D}\) if these were the true parameter values. Models with high likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})\) become more probable in the posterior distribution \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{D})\). This mirrors how we evaluate scientific theories in general. For example, we accept that the Earth is round because this model better explains ships that disappear hull-first and the circular shadow in lunar eclipses.

The Bayesian approach has several advantages for astronomical inference. It gives the full posterior distribution of the parameters, in addition to point estimates. It adds prior knowledge from previous studies or physical constraints in a direct way. The same approach works for a single observation or a large dataset. We can compare models through the evidence term \(p(\mathcal{D})\). It also allows hierarchical modeling, where parameters depend on higher-level parameters (Section 13.15).

These advantages suit astronomical data analysis, where we often have limited observations of unique phenomena and need to combine theoretical constraints with empirical evidence.

2.7 Bayesian Inference in Practice

Treating model parameters as random variables lets Bayesian inference handle limited data, even a single observation. We explore this with two examples that connect the theory to practice.

2.7.1 Inference with One Data Point

The Die Example

Consider four candidate models for the behavior of a die, which we call Fair, Bad, Worse, and Worst. Each model gives a specific probability for each outcome.

Table 2.1. Probability distributions for four die models. Each column is a hypothesis about the die, with Fair an unbiased die and each later model more biased toward lower numbers.
Outcome Fair Bad Worse Worst
6 1/6 1/8 1/12 1/20
5 1/6 1/8 1/12 1/20
4 1/6 1/6 1/8 1/10
3 1/6 1/6 1/6 1/10
2 1/6 5/24 5/24 1/5
1 1/6 5/24 1/3 1/2

Under the Fair model, each outcome has equal probability (\(p(\mathcal{D}=i|\boldsymbol{\theta}=\text{Fair})=1/6\) for all \(i\)). The Bad model is slightly biased toward lower numbers, and the Worse and Worst models are progressively more biased. For each model \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), the probabilities \(p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\) must sum to one, so each column of the table sums to one.

Now suppose we roll the die once and observe a 6. A frequentist approach can say little about a single roll, but Bayesian inference still gives a direct answer, a probability for each model. If we start with equal prior probabilities for each model (\(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\text{Fair}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\text{Bad}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\text{Worse}) = p(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\text{Worst}) = 1/4\)), Bayes’ theorem gives \[ p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\{6\}) \propto p(\{6\}|\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}). \]

Braces list the observed values, so \(\{6\}\) is one roll that gave a 6. Since we have equal priors \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \text{constant}\), the posterior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\mathcal{D}=\{6\})\) is proportional to the likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D}=\{6\}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\). We read this likelihood directly from the first row of the table, which gives the probability of rolling a 6 under each model. The evidence \(p(\mathcal{D})\) does not change our relative beliefs about the models, but it normalizes the posterior. Each column of the table, which is \(p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for a fixed \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), sums to one, but the rows do not. To get proper posterior probabilities, we divide the likelihoods by their sum over all models.

For our single roll of 6, the likelihoods are

  • The Fair model gives 1/6 = 0.167

  • The Bad model gives 1/8 = 0.125

  • The Worse model gives 1/12 = 0.083

  • The Worst model gives 1/20 = 0.050

The sum of these likelihoods is 0.425, so the posterior probabilities are

  • \(p(\text{Fair}|\{6\}) = 0.167/0.425 = 0.393\)

  • \(p(\text{Bad}|\{6\}) = 0.125/0.425 = 0.294\)

  • \(p(\text{Worse}|\{6\}) = 0.083/0.425 = 0.195\)

  • \(p(\text{Worst}|\{6\}) = 0.050/0.425 = 0.118\)

Our beliefs have shifted. We started with equal probability (0.25) for each model. After observing a single 6, we favor the Fair model (0.393) and consider the Worst model least likely (0.118). This makes sense, because a 6 is most consistent with the Fair model and least consistent with the Worst model. The Worst model gives much more probability to lower numbers.

Now suppose we observe two more outcomes, 1 and 4, so the likelihood becomes \(p(\{6,1,4\}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\). Die rolls are independent events, by the definition of independence we saw earlier, so this joint likelihood factorizes \[ p(\{6,1,4\}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) = p(\{6\}|\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\{1\}|\boldsymbol{\theta})p(\{4\}|\boldsymbol{\theta}). \]

We calculate this product for each model

  • For the Fair model, \(1/6 \times 1/6 \times 1/6 = 1/216 \approx 0.0046\)

  • For the Bad model, \(1/8 \times 5/24 \times 1/6 \approx 0.0043\)

  • For the Worse model, \(1/12 \times 1/3 \times 1/8 \approx 0.0035\)

  • For the Worst model, \(1/20 \times 1/2 \times 1/10 = 1/400 = 0.0025\)

After normalizing, the posterior probabilities are

  • \(p(\text{Fair}|\{6,1,4\}) \approx 0.31\)

  • \(p(\text{Bad}|\{6,1,4\}) \approx 0.29\)

  • \(p(\text{Worse}|\{6,1,4\}) \approx 0.23\)

  • \(p(\text{Worst}|\{6,1,4\}) \approx 0.17\)

The results are now more balanced between the models. The Fair model still has the highest probability, but the differences between models are smaller. This makes sense, because we observed a mixture of high (6) and low (1) values, which is somewhat consistent with all the models.

This example shows a main strength of Bayesian inference. If we can specify the probability of the observations under each model, which is the likelihood, we can update our beliefs even with minimal data. The same approach works for a single observation or for thousands of data points.

The Gaussian Mean Example

The same idea extends to continuous parameters. Consider measuring an astronomical quantity that follows a Gaussian distribution with known standard deviation \(\sigma\) and unknown mean \(\mu\). In the frequentist approach, we would take many measurements and use their average as our best estimate. But what if we only have one or two measurements?

Here the model parameter is the unknown mean \(\mu\). For simplicity, we fix \(\sigma=1\) to get a Gaussian with unit variance. Suppose we make a single measurement \(x = 6\). As in the die example, we apply Bayes’ theorem \[ p(\mu|\mathcal{D}=\{6\}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}=\{6\}|\mu)p(\mu). \]

We take a flat prior, so \(p(\mu)\) is a constant that does not depend on \(\mu\). Instead of a “look-up” table as for the die, the likelihood function \(p(\mathcal{D}=\{6\}|\mu)\) is \[ p(x=6|\mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(6-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]If we “propose” a value for \(\mu\), the probability density at the value 6 is the Gaussian PDF with this \(\mu\) evaluated at \(x=6\).

In Figure 2.9, different proposed values of \(\mu\) lead to different probability densities at \(x = 6\). When \(\mu = 2\), the density at \(x = 6\) is low, as the small value of the solid curve at \(x=6\) shows. When \(\mu = 5\), it is much higher, as the larger value of the dash-dot curve at \(x=6\) shows.

The bottom panel shows the likelihood for each proposed value of \(\mu\) given our single observation. With this flat prior, also called an uninformative prior, the likelihood is proportional to the posterior distribution. The maximum likelihood estimate, which is the value of \(\mu\) with the highest likelihood, is \(\mu = 6\). This makes sense, because with a single measurement and no informative prior, our best estimate of the mean is the measured value.

We fixed \(\sigma\) here on purpose. With a single data point, the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\sigma\) tends toward zero. This gives an infinitely narrow Gaussian centered at 6, unless we assume a reasonable prior that prevents this degenerate solution.

The problem becomes more interesting with more measurements. Suppose we make a second measurement \(x = 4\). We assume that the measurement errors are independent of each other, so we can multiply the individual likelihoods \[ p(x_1,x_2|\mu) = p(x_1|\mu)p(x_2|\mu). \]

In Figure 2.10, the bottom panel shows the joint likelihood, which is the probability of observing both measurements for each proposed value of \(\mu\). The maximum likelihood estimate has moved to \(\mu = 5\), the average of our two measurements. Each new measurement multiplies in another likelihood factor, so the posterior uses all the available information and becomes more concentrated.

If we add a third measurement, say \(x = 5\), the likelihood becomes \[ p(x_1,x_2,x_3|\mu) = p(x_1|\mu)p(x_2|\mu)p(x_3|\mu). \]The maximum likelihood estimate is still \(\mu = 5\), the average of our three measurements (4, 5, and 6). The likelihood curve becomes narrower still, which shows increased confidence in our estimate. Uncertainty decreases as we collect more data.

Implications for Scientific Inference

Treating model parameters as random variables lets us work with small or large amounts of evidence, whether or not we can repeat the experiment.

In the die example, Bayesian inference let us update our beliefs about different models as we gathered evidence. Even a single data point let us quantify the relative plausibility of each model. In the Gaussian example, our uncertainty about the mean decreased as we gathered more measurements, because the likelihood function became more concentrated.

Bayesian inference can also use prior knowledge. We used uninformative priors in our examples, but we could use more informative priors from previous studies or theory. For instance, if previous surveys suggest that the Gaussian mean is close to 3, we might use a prior \(p(\mu) = \mathcal{N}(\mu|3,1)\) (mean 3, variance 1). This pulls the posterior toward 3, especially when we have limited data. As we gather more data, the likelihood typically dominates the prior and reduces its influence on our conclusions.

Some see the need to specify priors as a weakness, but it can also be a strength. The balance between the prior \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) and the likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})\) matters for extraordinary claims in science. As Carl Sagan noted, “extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.” In Bayesian terms, we need a correspondingly strong likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D} | \boldsymbol{\theta})\) to overcome a strong skeptical prior, such as our prior against faster-than-light travel. This balance expresses both the open-mindedness and the skepticism that scientific work needs.

The die and Gaussian examples are deliberately simple, to show the core principles of Bayesian inference. The same principles apply to complex models with many parameters. There the posterior is a high-dimensional distribution over parameter space. The logic of updating our beliefs from observed data stays the same in the more sophisticated machine learning methods that follow.

2.8 Tutorials: Cluster Detection and Binary Orbits

Two tutorials apply the Poisson distribution, the likelihood, Bayes’ theorem and marginalization to astronomy. The first searches for intermediate-mass black holes through their star clusters. The second reads the shape of a binary orbit from one snapshot. The full tutorials can be found at https://statml.org/ as 2a and 2b.

Finding Star Clusters

Astronomers search the Milky Way halo for intermediate-mass black holes, which lie between stellar-mass and supermassive ones. Theory predicts that each one keeps a cluster of stars around it, an excess over the smooth halo background. A search for such excesses can find candidate black holes.

To find a cluster, we first need a model of the stars without one. Stars at random positions fall independently of each other (Section 2.5). The count in a small window therefore follows the Poisson distribution (Section 2.3), whose mean is the density times the area. This gives the likelihood of the count at each position under the background alone (Section 2.7).

With this model, a cluster is a place where the count is far above the average, so the likelihood of the count is very small. In a simulated field the two clusters stand out to the eye (Figure 2.11a). The likelihood of the count at each position replaces this judgment with a number (Figure 2.11b). A detection is therefore a statement about probability, and it depends on the background model. A search that finds no cluster also limits the number of such black holes, because each one would leave a very unlikely count.

Reading a Binary Orbit from One Snapshot

Binary stars give us stellar masses through Kepler’s Third Law (Section 2.1), and their orbits record how they formed. Measuring an orbit needs observations over multiple orbital periods, which is too slow for large samples. A snapshot gives one angle \(\gamma\), between the relative position and velocity of the two stars. Figure 2.12a colors an orbit by this angle. On a circular orbit it is \(90^\circ\) at each point. On an eccentric orbit it changes, and the eccentricity \(e\) measures how elongated it is.

Physics gives the angle from the eccentricity and the orbital phase. The phase tells where the stars are along the orbit, and we do not know it when we observe. We want the reverse, \(e\) from the angle. Bayes’ theorem (Section 2.6) does this, and marginalization (Section 2.5) removes the unknown phase by averaging over phases that we treat as equally likely. With a uniform prior (Section 2.7), the posterior of \(e\) is proportional to the likelihood (Figure 2.12b).

The likelihood has a simple geometry. The larger the eccentricity, the farther the angle can swing from \(90^\circ\) (Figure 2.12a). An angle far from \(90^\circ\) therefore needs a large eccentricity, so one angle sets a lower limit on \(e\). In Figure 2.12b each posterior starts at this limit, which is higher for angles farther from \(90^\circ\), and has a long tail above it. The angle has a measurement error, and marginalizing over the true angle blurs the posterior (dashed).

Many binaries reveal the eccentricity distribution of a population, which depends on how the binaries formed and evolved. Physics predicts the data, an unknown such as the phase is marginalized, and Bayes’ theorem turns the data into what we want to know.

Further Reading

Bayes (1763) wrote a posthumous essay on inverse probability. Jaynes (2003) treats probability theory as an extension of logic and links Bayesian methods to science. Box and Tiao (1973) treat Bayesian methods systematically. Gelman et al. (2013) give worked examples. Sivia and Skilling (2006) give an introduction for physical scientists. Loredo (1992) argued for Bayesian methods in astronomy with examples, including supernova neutrinos. Gregory (2005b) compares frequentist and Bayesian approaches. Trotta (2008) reviews Bayesian inference and model selection in cosmology. Eadie et al. (2023) discuss Bayesian methods in astronomy. Thrane and Talbot (2019) cover parameter estimation, model selection and hierarchical models in gravitational wave astronomy. Greene et al. (2021) searched for clusters around wandering black holes (first tutorial). Hwang et al. (2022) measured wide binary eccentricities from single observations (second tutorial).
